idiom_name: functions over an immutable struct returning the same struct by value
implementation_notes: C has no operator overloading for user-defined types, so a closed operation is an ordinary function declared next to the type in one header: money_t money_add(money_t a, money_t b) returns a new value of the same struct, and there is no way for a call site to see the representation if the fields are opaque. What replaces the classic structure is therefore a hand-written convention: one canonical representation (integer minor units plus currency code) so the invariant can be re-established in each function, parameters taken by value or as const pointers, and the result returned as a value rather than written through an out-parameter. The classic function form is still the right one whenever the struct is small and copyable; for large or variable-size values (strings, buffers) the same shape forces either allocation or a caller-supplied destination, and the closure survives only in the type signature, not in the memory model.
pitfalls: Returning a large struct by value copies it on every combination; if the type grows, the operation degrades into an out-parameter form and stops reading as closed - keep value types small or document the change.
No canonical representation means no closure: if an amount is stored as (major, exponent) without normalisation, two equal values can produce different results from the same operation.

char * is not closed: concatenating two strings allocates, so the operation must either return a newly allocated buffer (ownership trap) or write into a caller-supplied one (aliasing trap); prefer fixed-capacity or arena-owned types for domain values.
Signed overflow in C is undefined behaviour, so an addition that is 'closed' in type terms can still trap or wrap silently - use explicit range checks.
